clinicalPearls: An inflammation of subcutaneous fat caused directly by microbial infection, encompassing bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal and, rarely, parasitic organisms.
It should be suspected when panniculitis is accompanied by fever, systemic upset, immunosuppression, ulceration, abscess formation or a suppurative, draining quality.
Immunocompromised patients (including those on biologics, chemotherapy or corticosteroids, and diabetics) are at particular risk and may show atypical or opportunistic organisms.
Histology characteristically shows a mixed septal and lobular panniculitis with neutrophils, sometimes suppuration, necrosis and, in mycobacterial or fungal disease, granulomas.
Special stains (Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, PAS, Grocott) and, crucially, tissue culture of a deep biopsy are needed because organisms may be sparse.
So-called bottom-heavy inflammation, deep dermal and subcutaneous extension, vascular proliferation and interstitial neutrophils are histological clues that favour an infective cause.
Empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy may be required in the septic patient while cultures are pending, then narrowed to the identified organism.
A deep incisional biopsy sent for both histology and microbiology, rather than a superficial punch, is the single most useful diagnostic step.
reference.pathophysiology: Infective panniculitis arises when micro-organisms reach the subcutaneous fat, either by direct inoculation through trauma or injection, by contiguous spread from overlying skin or deeper structures, or haematogenously in bacteraemic or immunocompromised hosts. Microbial proliferation and released enzymes and toxins damage adipocytes and vasculature, and the host mounts a predominantly neutrophilic and, for intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria and fungi, granulomatous inflammatory response. Fat necrosis, abscess formation and septal and lobular inflammation follow. The pattern and intensity of the reaction depend on the organism and the immune competence of the host, so immunosuppressed patients may show attenuated inflammation yet abundant organisms.
additionalInvestigations: deep incisional biopsy for histopathology with special stains (Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, PAS, Grocott)
tissue culture for bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi from a deep specimen
full blood count and assessment of immune status (including HIV testing where relevant)
imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to define the extent of deep infection or abscess
polymerase chain reaction or molecular assays for fastidious organisms
review of injections, travel, animal exposure and immunosuppressive therapy
redFlags: sepsis with fever, hypotension or rapidly spreading induration
necrotising soft-tissue infection requiring urgent surgical debridement
immunosuppression with atypical or disseminated infection
fluctuance, discharge or abscess formation requiring drainage
failure to improve on empirical antibiotics, suggesting mycobacterial, fungal or resistant organisms
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the organism, host immune status and timeliness of treatment; most immunocompetent patients recover fully with appropriate antimicrobial therapy, whereas deep, necrotising or opportunistic infections in immunocompromised hosts carry appreciable morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Treating an infective panniculitis as a sterile inflammatory panniculitis with immunosuppression, worsening the infection.
Relying on a superficial biopsy that misses deep organisms and yields negative cultures.
Omitting tissue culture and special stains when only routine histology is requested.
Underestimating atypical organisms in immunocompromised patients.
Missing an evolving necrotising infection that requires surgical rather than purely medical management.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, current edition
management: Direct treatment at the cultured organism: empirical broad-spectrum antibacterials pending deep tissue culture, narrowed to targeted therapy, with prolonged multidrug antimycobacterial regimens for mycobacterial disease and systemic antifungals (azole or amphotericin-based agents) for fungal panniculitis
Drain and debride abscesses and necrotic subcutaneous fat surgically, with repeated exploration where suppuration persists
Provide supportive wound care, analgesia and management of systemic sepsis
Address host immunosuppression: review and reduce corticosteroids, biologics or chemotherapy where feasible, optimise glycaemic control in diabetics and treat underlying HIV
Undertake urgent surgical exploration with broad empirical antimicrobial cover for necrotising or rapidly progressive deep infection
Coordinate prolonged, organism-directed treatment across dermatology, infectious diseases, microbiology and surgery
